Find the minimum positive integer \( n \) for which there exists a partition of the set \(\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}\) into two non-empty disjoint subsets \( A \) and \( B \) such that for all integers \( k \) with \( 0 < k < n \), the following conditions hold:

Alice and Bob play a game on a 100-by-100 grid, where squares are initially painted white. They take turns; Alice goes first. On each player's turn, they pick a white square and paint it blue. However, the square must either be in the top row or the leftmost column, and when this square is painted, every square in its row and column that is also initially white gets painted blue. Alice wins if there exists a path entirely of blue squares that connects the top-left corner to the bottom-right corner. Alice and Bob play optimally. The game ends in a tie if Bob can force the game into such a state. Determine who wins.

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of integers. Initially, each cell is white. Alice starts the game by coloring any chosen cell black. From that point on, each player in his or her turn must choose a cell that was previously uncolored and has exactly two black cells adjacent to it and color it black. The game stops when either no more moves are available or a player is unable to make a move. Determine the maximum number of black cells that can exist on the grid at the end of the game, ensuring each configuration follows the rules correctly.

Alice and Bob play a game on a regular hexagon grid, alternating turns placing vertices; Alice starts first. Once the grid is fully filled with vertices, Bob scores the number of regular hexagons that contain two black vertices and two white vertices (two vertices being adjacent). Alice and Bob both play optimally. Alice can guarantee that Bob's score will be at most $n$, what is the minimum value of $n$?

Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(1) = 17$ and $P(17) = 1$. Suppose further that for any integer $n$, $P(n)$ is divisible by a unique prime $q_n$ (which may depend on $n$). What is the minimum number of distinct prime factors that $P(n)$ can have for some integer $n > 1$?

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite 2D plane. Initially, Alice places a pebble at some point \((a_1, b_1)\). In each step, Alice picks a new point \((a_i, b_i)\) at which the pebble is not currently placed, computes the midpoint \(M_i\) of \((a_i, b_i)\) and the current position of the pebble, and moves the pebble to \(M_i\). Bob must then guess whether Alice intends to move the pebble horizontally (to \((a_{i+1}, b_i)\)) or vertically (to \((a_i, b_{i+1})\)) next. Bob’s prediction is based only on the current and previous positions of the pebble. Determine all possible integers \(n > 1\) for which there exists a strategy for Bob that guarantees he can guess correctly at least \(\frac{1}{n}\) of the times, regardless of Alice’s starting point and moves.

There are $n$ students, each student has three numbers $a$, $b$, $c$ $(1 \leq a, b, c \leq n, a, b, c \text{ are distinct integers})$ written on their forehead such that no two students share all three of these numbers. They will write their name on three pieces of paper based on the given $a$, $b$, and $c$, and place them in three cups placed in front of their own table. They won’t be able to see their own forehead until they have time to rest. After they rest, all of the papers from all students’ cups will be opened simultaneously and dropped on the floor.

The probability that no paper gets closer to the student who originally wrote it than the next nearest student is given by $P_n$. What is the least value of $n$ for which $P_n > \frac{1}{2}$?

In the land of Geometria, there is a mystical rectangular garden, whose perimeter is 140 meters and its diagonal is 50 meters. The garden is surrounded by a path of uniform width, and the outer edge of this path forms a rectangle with twice the area of the original garden. Find the width of the path.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = P(1) = 2023 \) and \( P(n) \) is prime for infinitely many positive integers \( n \). Determine the smallest possible value of \( |P(10)| \).

For a fixed integer n ≥ 3, let P(x) be a monic polynomial of degree n with integer coefficients. Define the "orbit" of an integer x as the sequence (x_0, x_1, ..., x_n) where x_0 = x, x_1 = |P(x_0)|, x_2 = |P(x_1)|, ..., x_n = |P(x_{n-1})|. For each n, there exists a smallest integer d_n ≥ 0 such that no two distinct points in the orbit of any integer x can differ by at most d_n (in absolute value). Find the minimum value of d_n for n ≥ 3.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = P(1) = 1 \) and for all integers \( n \geq 2 \), \( P(n) \) is divisible by either 2 or 3, but never both. Find the minimum possible degree of \( P(x) \).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 3 \). Suppose further that there exists an integer \( n \geq 2 \) for which the following three conditions hold:
1. \( P(n) = 0 \),
2. The degree of \( P(x) \) is a prime number,
3. For every integer \( k \) with \( 0 < k < n \), the polynomial \( Q_k(x) = P(x^k) \) has at least one root in the interval \( (-n, n) \).

Determine the smallest possible value of \( n \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite 2-dimensional grid of real numbers. They take turns. Alice goes first.

Initially, the center square (0,0) contains the real number 0. Also, consider a rule: if any square (x,y) contains the real number k, then any other square (x+n,y+n) must contain the real number k+n^2 for any integer n.

The players must choose an unused square that has not been used in the game yet. Once a square is occupied, it can never be used again. The square chosen must follow the rule mentioned. On Alice’s turn, she chooses a square that has not been used yet and places the least positive integer not present anywhere in the grid. On Bob’s turn, he chooses a square that has not been used yet and places the least negative integer not present anywhere in the grid.

The players continue this way until all squares are filled. After all squares are filled, the players score points. For each square (x,y) that contains the number k, the score for that square is |k - x - y|.

The player with the higher total score wins. If Alice and Bob both play optimally, determine who will win the game and by how many points.

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \( P(0) = 1 \), \( P(1) = 2 \), and for all integers \( n \geq 2 \), the following holds:
\[ P(n) = P(n-1) + n! + (n-1)! \]
Determine the smallest positive integer \( k \) for which there exists an integer \( a \) such that \( P(a) = k! \).

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite 2D plane with a starting point at (0,0). They take turns performing moves. In each move, a player selects a point (x,y) on the plane and places a stone at that point. No two stones can share the same coordinates. Each stone placed at (x,y) earns the placing player x^2 + y^2 points. The game ends when one player cannot place a new stone without overlapping an existing one. Alice starts first. Find the total number of distinct possible games if Alice and Bob both play optimally. Your answer should be the sum of all possible final scores divided by the least common multiple of all pairwise differences between Alice and Bob's optimal scores.
Let \(P(x)\) be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that \(P(1) = 2023\) and \(P(2) = 2024\). Determine the maximum number of integer roots \(P(x)\) can have.

Find the smallest positive integer \( n \) such that the polynomial \( P(x) = x^n + x^{n-1} + \ldots + x + 1 \) is divisible by the polynomial \( Q(x) = x^5 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + 1 \) when evaluated at all 9th roots of unity (excluding 1).

Alice and Bob play a game on an infinite grid of unit squares. Alice starts by placing a token at the origin (0,0). In each turn, the player whose turn it is moves the token to a square that is at most \(\sqrt{2}\) units away from its current position, including diagonally adjacent squares. The player then draws a line segment connecting the old position of the token to its new position. The game ends when any square on the grid has been covered by a line segment at least twice. If the game is played optimally, what is the minimum number of turns required to end the game?

Let \(P(x)\) be a monic polynomial with integer coefficients such that \(P(1) = 17\) and \(P(n) \equiv 0 \pmod{17}\) for infinitely many integers \(n\). If \(Q(x) = P(x) + x^2 - 3x + 2\) and \(R(x) = Q(x) + x^3 - 2x^2 + x - 1\), prove that there exists an integer \(m\) such that \(R(m) \equiv 0 \pmod{17}\) but \(P(m) \not\equiv 0 \pmod{17}\).

Let \( P(x) \) be a polynomial with integer coefficients, such that \( P(0) = 1 \) and \( P(1) = 2023 \). If for every integer \( n \geq 0 \), \( P(n) \) is divisible by 2023 if and only if \( n \) is divisible by 2023, find the minimum degree of \( P(x) \).
Let $P(x)$ be a polynomial with integer coefficients such that $P(0) = P(1) = 1$ and $P(n)$ is a perfect square for every positive integer $n$. Determine all possible values of $P(2)$.
